Ranking — among candidates that clear the floor. Primary: answer_correctness , candidate against candidate, computed as follows. compare_runs.py compares one run file against one baseline file and cannot average two runs per model, so the primary statistic comes from a small analysis script adapted from the Qwen3.8 comparison's model_subsets.py , frozen with the pre-registration (its file hash recorded there): per question, each finalist's score is the mean of its two runs; d = A − B per question, over the bank questions scored in all four finalist runs; SE = standard deviation of d / √n; σ = the larger of the two finalists' run-to-run spread (the absolute difference between a model's two run means), as in the Qwen3.8 comparison; a difference counts only if |mean d| exceeds both 2·SE and 2·σ, and the per-run pairs (A run 1 vs B run 1, A run 2 vs B run 2, from compare_runs.py ) agree in sign. compare_runs.py still runs on every per-run pair, for its validity gates (G3–G10) and the G8 report below. Inside that noise, the tie is broken in order by faithfulness , mean seconds per question, give-up answers, then the simpler operation (fewer GPUs, no image patches). With a single candidate in Phase 2, there is nothing to rank: it is adopted if it clears the floor. compare_runs.py 's G8 row (anchors, plus "no other metric regressed past one noise unit") is reported for the finalist pair, with the runner-up as baseline and --noise-runs set to the runner-up's two runs, so every metric has a noise floor; where a metric's two-run σ is 0, --noise-floor takes the larger of the two finalists' two-run spreads for it, recorded as a deviation (the Qwen3.8 comparison's procedure). Without a floor, G8 skips that metric and can read clean when it was never tested. If the correctness winner shows a G8 regression on another metric, the choice goes to the operator with both rows in front of them, recorded in the ledger — it is not automatic either way. G8 is not a hard gate here because on 2026-10-12 it raised an alarm on Qwen3.6 against its own second run (easy-anchor scores, and answer_correctness against a two-run noise estimate of 0.0025). Against Qwen3.6, G8 is reported as part of the cost of the policy. 3. Cost of the policy — reported, not gated. Each candidate minus Qwen3.6 on every RAGAS metric, source accuracy, speed and judge cost per run, so the operator can say what the move cost. context_precision and context_recall can move too: the model writes the search queries. If no candidate clears the floor: the operator chooses between relaxing the floor; the Gemma 4 port (§9); and the Anthropic standby already configured in dev.yaml ( default_provider: anthropic , US-developed) — which sends every question off the host and is billed per token, so it is a decision, not a default. 7. Cost and time per run What costs money. Only the judge — the Bedrock Claude Sonnet 4.5 model that grades each answer. GPU time is on-prem and carries no per-run charge; downloads are free. Judge prices are Bedrock list ($3.30 / $16.50 per million input / output tokens); HUIT billing may differ. Measured anchors (2026-10-12, 109 questions, same stack and judge): Model Wall time per run Judge calls Judge cost per run Per question Qwen3.6-35B-A3B 1 h 58 min – 3 h 05 min 1,697 / 1,729 $27.48 / $27.85 ~$0.25 Qwen3.8-27B (dense) 3 h 05 min – 3 h 19 min 2,647 / 2,735 $45.88 / $47.31 ~$0.43 Judge cost tracks how much the answers say (more statements to check, more judge calls), so a candidate's cost is unknown until it runs; the two measured models bracket it at $0.25–0.43 per question. Wall time is the model's answering time (109 × seconds per question) plus judging and start-up, which took 55–131 min in the four measured runs. A finalist that meets the §6 speed floor (mean ≤ 60 s) answers in under 1 h 50 min, so no Phase 2 candidate run should exceed ~4 h. Run Questions Wall time (est.) Judge cost (est.) Phase 0, load and fit — per candidate — ~2 h, plus the download (15–40 GB) $0 Phase 1.1–1.3, functional checks — per candidate a handful ~1 h < $1 Phase 1.4 pilot — Qwen3.6 reference (once) 30 + 5 anchors ~30–50 min ~$9 Phase 1.4 pilot — Nemotron 3 Nano or 3.5 Lightning 30 + 5 anchors ~30–55 min $9–15 Phase 1.4 pilot — Mistral Small 3.2 or Granite 4.1 30 + 5 anchors ~50–70 min $9–15 Phase 1.4 pilot — Llama 3.3 70B 30 + 5 anchors ~1.25–2 h $9–15 Phase 2 ingest (only if the old document set cannot be recovered) — ~1.5 h $0 Phase 2 full run — Qwen3.6 (×2, the brackets) 109 2–3 h each ~$28 each Phase 2 full run — a Nemotron finalist 109 ~2–3 h $28–47 Phase 2 full run — a Mistral or Granite finalist 109 ~3–4 h (dense Qwen3.8-27B took 3 h 05–3 h 19) $28–47 Phase 2 full run — Llama 3.3 70B (if it reaches Phase 2) 109 ≤ 4 h if it meets the floor; at its likely speed (est. 5–7 h) the pilot cuts it first $28–47 Identifier and capacity probes — per model 200 draws / 40 questions ~1 h $0 (no judge) In-house 4-bit quantization (§9 item 6, if chosen) — per candidate — est. a few hours for 24–32B, longer for 70B $0 Phase 3 redeploy — ~1 h (re-index) $0 Whole trial, five candidates screened and two finalists: pilots ~$55–85 (Qwen3.6 plus five candidates); Phase 2 ~$170–245 (two Qwen3.6 runs plus four finalist runs); about $225–330 in judge spend , and roughly 15–27 hours of GPU time for Phase 2 (six runs back to back plus probes), most of it unattended overnight. 8. Ledger Candidate Phase reached Result Date Evidence Llama 3.3 70B Instruct — (Phase 0, last) — — — Gemma 4 31B IT blocked before Phase 0 no model code in the image; head size 512 not supported by its V100 flash-attention backend 2026-10-13 §2 Command R+ 08-2024 blocked before Phase 0 no vLLM tool parser for its format; needs all four GPUs and more disk; non-commercial license 2026-10-13 §2 Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B — (Phase 0, first) — — — Mistral Small 3.2 24B — — — — Granite 4.1 30B — — — — Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B — (needs a loader patch first) — — — gpt-oss-20b, Phi-4, Llama 4 Scout ruled out at screening fp16 overflow / 16k context / too large 2026-10-13 §3 9. Decisions Made (operator, 2026-10-13): - The move off Qwen is policy; candidates cannot be Chinese-developed. The winner is the best allowed model that clears the usability floor (§1, §6). - Qwen3.8 stopped and disabled; its weights deleted. Open: 1. The usability floor in §6 — confirm or change the numbers before the first pilot, when the rule is frozen: what is the slowest, least reliable chat you would ship? 2. Gemma 4: fund a separate spike — port the Gemma 4 architecture into the Volta fork and (most likely) extend its attention kernel to head size 512, with its own estimate and the rebuild risk of #286 (the image has no build recipe) — covering both 31B and 26B-A4B; or drop Gemma 4. 3. Command R+: recommend dropping. Trialling it needs all of: a tool parser written for its output format, a trial window with production failed over to the Anthropic standby (it needs all four GPUs), deleting more of the model cache, and a legal reading of CC-BY-NC for institutional use — for a model two generations old. 4. Fallback if nothing clears the floor (§6): relax the floor, fund the Gemma 4 port, or accept the off-host Anthropic standby. 5. License sign-off for the winner. Apache 2.0, OpenMDW-1.1 and the Llama 3.3 Community License are routine; the NVIDIA Nemotron Open Model License (Nemotron 3 Nano) adds an attribution notice and terminates if the user brings an IP suit against NVIDIA. 6. Who made the 4-bit weights. The policy is about who made the model, and a 4-bit checkpoint is the developer's weights re-packaged by whoever quantized them. Every checkpoint in §3 except Google's and Red Hat's comes from an individual Hugging Face account. Production's Qwen3.6 file ( palmfuture/… ) is one too, so this is not a new exposure, but it should be a decision. Options per candidate: a vendor-published 4-bit where one exists (Red Hat's Llama 3.3); otherwise quantize in-house from the developer's official repo with llm-compressor or GPTQModel on GPUs 0–1 (estimate: hours for a 24–32B model, longer for 70B); or accept the community checkpoint. Record the choice in the ledger.

docs.text: Status: draft for operator review, 2026-10-13. Nothing has run. The decision rule is set (§6); its usability-floor numbers are proposals until the operator confirms them. The whole rule — floor, pilot cut and ranking — is then frozen into a timestamped pre-registration before the first Phase 1.4 pilot , because the pilot already applies the floor and the cut, as the Qwen3.8 comparison did ( /scratch/a2rchi/bench-runs/ragas-qwen38/PREREGISTRATION.md ). Feature under test: the answering model, services.chat_app.providers.*.default_model / services.benchmarking.model : palmfuture/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-GPTQ-Int4 → the best allowed candidate (§3). Everything else — code, prompt, corpus, judge, sampling, context window — is held fixed.
docs.title: Answering-model replacement: moving archi off Qwen3.6 (2026-10)

docs.text: Policy (operator, 2026-10-13): archi must move off Qwen, and the replacement cannot be a Chinese-developed model. Qwen3.6 leaves whatever it scores, so the question is not "is a candidate as good as Qwen3.6" but: Which allowed open-weights model is the best answering model archi can run on the V100 host? — the best of what is allowed, as long as it is good enough to ship. That gives a two-part rule (§6): Usability floor. A candidate must be fast and reliable enough for chat — absolute numbers, not "within X of Qwen3.6", because the move is not optional. Ranking. Among candidates that clear the floor, the one with the best answers wins. Qwen3.6 stays in the benchmark as a reference, not a gate. It is the only yardstick on the same document set and it detects drift between runs. Each candidate's score minus Qwen3.6's is reported as the cost of the policy : how much answer quality the move gives up, if any. Precedent. The 2026-10-12 Qwen3.8 comparison supplies the method this plan reuses (same document set, two runs per model, a plan fixed before the first run). Qwen3.8 itself is out under the policy.
docs.title: 1. The question, and how the winner is chosen

docs.text: Checked on archi.rc.fas.harvard.edu on 2026-10-13 against the Volta vLLM image that serves both models today ( /scratch/a2rchi/sifs/vllm_volta.sif , vLLM fork 1.1.0, transformers 4.57.6). That image is a hand-built Volta port with no build recipe on disk (see #286), so "does the image support it" is a hard constraint, not a version bump. Claim in the candidate list Finding Evidence Gemma 4 31B "fits on one V100 … maximum generation speed" Cannot be served on this image. Two independent gaps. (1) No Gemma 4 model code: upstream support arrived in vLLM 0.19.1 with transformers ≥ 5.5, and the image has neither, so vLLM 's generic transformers fallback is out too. (2) The image's V100 flash-attention backend handles head sizes 64, 128 and 256 only; Gemma 4's 10 full-attention layers use 512, and no other backend in the image was verified to cover it. Serving it means porting the architecture into the Volta fork and, most likely, extending the kernel. Only the Gemma 4 tool parser ships in the image. image registry.py lists Gemma 1–3/3n only; transformers.models.gemma4 absent; flash_attn_v100.py:970 get_supported_head_sizes() → [64, 128, 256] ; HF config.json global_head_dim: 512 Gemma 4 31B: faster than today Wrong comparison. Qwen3.6 is a mixture-of-experts model that reads ~3B parameters per generated token; dense Gemma 4 31B reads all 31B. Dropping tensor parallelism removes the PCIe sync cost but not the ~10× more weight traffic. The nearest measured case, dense Qwen3.8-27B on this host, was 2× slower on average and 3–4× slower at p90. Qwen3.6 config: 256 experts, 8 active; Qwen3.8 COMPARISON.md Gemma 4 31B "8-bit or 4-bit fits on a 32 GB V100" 4-bit only: the 8-bit checkpoint is 35.1 GB, more than the card. Gemma 4 was trained in bf16, which V100 lacks; fp16 overflow is confirmed in its vision encoder and documented for Gemma 3 text, unverified for Gemma 4 text. cyankiwi/gemma-4-31B-it-AWQ-8bit ; vLLM #40290 Llama 3.3 70B 4-bit "~40 GB across two V100s … plenty of VRAM for RAG context" Fits, but context memory is tight compared with today. Llama 3.3 70B keeps 320 KiB of cache per token; Qwen3.6 keeps ~20 KiB (only 10 of its 40 layers use full attention). Two cards at the 0.88 memory cap leave roughly 50k tokens of cache after weights: under two full 32k-token conversations at once. Qwen3.6 config.json ; Llama 3.3: 80 layers × 8 KV heads × 128 dim × 2 × 2 bytes Command R+ 4-bit "~60 GB fits cleanly across two 32 GB GPUs" Does not fit on two. Two cards at the 0.88 cap give 56.3 GiB for weights and cache; the 4-bit checkpoints are 54.6–60.4 GiB (58.6–64.9 GB), leaving at most ~1.7 GiB for working memory and cache — one 32k-token request alone needs 8 GiB. It needs all four GPUs, which means taking production Qwen3.6 down for the trial. 2 × 32 768 MiB × 0.88; the 0.95 cap crashed production in June (#43) Command R+ "purpose-built for … multi-step tool use" vLLM cannot parse its tool calls. No vLLM parser reads Command R+'s tool-call format (an Action: line followed by a JSON block); the image's cohere_command3 / cohere_command4 parsers target the later Command A models, and they also need the cohere_melody package, which is not installed. archi's agent cannot search without one. vLLM tool-calling docs; import cohere_melody → ModuleNotFoundError in the image Command R+ as a current model The newest version is 08-2024, superseded by Command A (03-2025, 111B, same license) and Command A+ (05-2026, Apache 2.0, but ~132 GB at 4-bit, more than all four cards). Its license is CC-BY-NC 4.0, a "research release": internal university use is plausibly non-commercial, but that needs a legal reading. Cohere model cards "AWQ or GPTQ" Both run on V100 in this fork (GPTQ from compute capability 6.0; AWQ from 7.0 through a fork-specific kernel). Marlin kernels (7.5+) and MXFP4 (8.0+) do not. Repo names are unreliable: several "AWQ"/"GPTQ" repos are really compressed-tensors, so read quantization_config.quant_method in config.json before downloading. get_min_capability() in the image's quantization modules Disk: the Qwen3.8 weights (20 GB) were deleted on 2026-10-13, leaving 54 GB free on /scratch — room for a 4-bit Llama 3.3 70B (~40 GB) but not a 4-bit Command R+ (~58 GB). The further candidates screened in §3 are 15–18 GB each.
docs.title: 2. What the candidate descriptions get wrong on this host

docs.text: Llama 3.3 70B Instruct Gemma 4 31B IT Command R+ 08-2024 Developer, license Meta (US); Llama 3.3 Community License + acceptable-use policy Google (US); Apache 2.0 Cohere (Canada); CC-BY-NC 4.0 + Cohere Labs acceptable-use policy Released 2024-12-06 (still Meta's newest 70B; Llama 4 has no dense 70B) 2026-04-02 2024-08 Shape dense, 70B, 128k context dense, 30.7B, text + image, 256k context dense, 104B, 128k context Cache per token (Qwen3.6 ≈ 20 KiB) 320 KiB ~80 KiB on 10 full layers (40 KiB if keys and values are stored once) + ~0.8 GiB fixed per request for the 1,024-token sliding layers 256 KiB 4-bit checkpoint RedHatAI/Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct-quantized.w4a16 — Red Hat (US), compressed-tensors, symmetric, group 128, ~39.5 GB (verified 2026-10-13); community GPTQ alternatives clowman/…-GPTQ-Int4 , shuyuej/…-GPTQ , 39.8 GB google/gemma-4-31B-it-qat-w4a16-ct , 23.3 GB, compressed-tensors (Google's own quantization-aware release) nejumi/c4ai-command-r-plus-08-2024-GPTQ-Int4-calib-ja-1k , 58.6 GB (calibrated on Japanese text) Runs on the current image yes — model code and head size 128 supported no — no model code; head size 512 not supported by the V100 flash-attention backend model code yes; does not fit two GPUs Tool parser in the image llama3_json (no parallel calls; vLLM warns of malformed arguments). Its recommended chat template is not in the image — bind examples/tool_chat_template_llama3.1_json.jinja from the vLLM repo. gemma4 none for this model's format These three were the starting list. Because the move is mandatory, the field is every allowed model the host can run, so a second screen (2026-10-13) checked the other allowed families the image has code for, with the same tests: exists at this size, license, a 4-bit checkpoint whose quant_method V100 loads, a tool parser in the image, attention head size ≤ 256, and fit on GPUs 0–1. Image-side facts were checked inside vllm_volta.sif ; the rest comes from each model's config.json and model card. NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B IBM Granite 4.1 30B Mistral Small 3.2 24B Instruct (2506) Developer, license NVIDIA (US); NVIDIA Nemotron Open Model License — commercial use allowed, requires an attribution notice, ends if the user sues NVIDIA over IP NVIDIA (US); OpenMDW-1.1 (permissive, Linux Foundation) IBM (US); Apache 2.0 Mistral AI (France); Apache 2.0 Released 2025-12-15 2026-08-11 2026-04-29 2025-06 Shape hybrid mixture-of-experts: 31.6B total, 3.5B per token ; 52 layers = 23 Mamba2 + 23 expert + 6 attention same as Nemotron 3 Nano dense, 30B dense, 24B Cache per token (Qwen3.6 ≈ 20 KiB) 6 KiB 6 KiB 256 KiB 160 KiB 4-bit checkpoint stelterlab/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B-AWQ — compressed-tensors despite the name, 17.8 GB (a GPTQ one exists but quantizes unusual layers) SergiioB/Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-GPTQ-INT4-G64-sym — real GPTQ, 18.1 GB drawais/Granite-4.1-30B-AWQ-INT4 — compressed-tensors despite the name, 15.5 GB gratex/mistral-small-3.2-24b-Instruct-GPTQ-W4A16 — real GPTQ, 15.1 GB Tool parser qwen3_coder — the parser production uses today qwen3_coder hermes or granite4 (IBM names none for 4.1; both in the image) mistral (its mistral_common dependency is in the image) Image check model code with expert layers present model code present, but it reads the older hybrid_override_pattern config key and Lightning's config uses layers_block_type : expect a loader patch GraniteForCausalLM present Mistral model code present Open risk (Phase 0 decides) Mamba2 kernels on V100; 4-bit expert layers in compressed-tensors format on V100 (the image has a V100-specific path, untested here); fp16 as Nemotron 3 Nano, plus the loader patch fp16; dense-30B speed (dense Qwen3.8-27B was 2× slower) fp16; weakest published tool calling of the four Published scores (self-reported) BFCL v4 tool calling 53.8 vs 46.4 for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B itself: long-document reasoning (AA-LCR) 52.0 vs 61.1; instruction following (IFBench) 71.9 vs 63.7 BFCL v3 73.7 vs 65.1 for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct BFCL v4 37.2 vs 41.4 for Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct Publisher scores are leads, not evidence: they set the testing order and nothing else. Only NVIDIA's Lightning table compares against Qwen3.6 directly, and it shows a real gap on long-document reasoning, the closest public proxy for this job — an early estimate of the cost of the policy. Ruled out: - OpenAI gpt-oss-20b — fp16 overflow is documented in its expert layers, its native 4-bit format (MXFP4) needs newer GPUs, and the only V100-loadable conversion is of unknown origin. - Microsoft Phi-4 — 16,384-token context, below the 32,768 archi needs. - Llama 4 Scout — 62.7–64.9 GB at 4-bit: over both the memory cap and the free disk. - Excluded by policy although the image supports them: DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, MiniMax, ERNIE, Seed. Reserves (tested only if the candidates below fail): IBM Granite 4.0 H-Small (superseded by Granite 4.1 on tool calling; carries the Mamba and expert-layer risks with no GPTQ checkpoint) and AI2 OLMo 3.1 32B Instruct (weakest tool calling of the set; its sliding-window layers fall off the image's fast V100 attention path). Order. Phase 0 is hours per model, so every candidate gets it, most promising and smallest first; the 30-question pilot (Phase 1.4) then picks two for Phase 2. Nemotron 3 Nano — Qwen3.6's speed class, production's own tool parser, a tiny context cache. Mistral Small 3.2 — the lowest kernel risk: real GPTQ, plain dense model. Granite 4.1 30B — the strongest published tool-calling score; dense, so slower. Nemotron 3.5 Lightning — after a loader patch; the newest, and per NVIDIA the closest to Qwen3.6. Llama 3.3 70B — last: its 40 GB of weights need the others' deleted first, and it is the most likely to miss the speed floor. Two fit on disk at a time with Phase 0.1's 10 GB margin (Nemotron 3 Nano + Mistral Small 3.2 ≈ 33 GB of the 54 GB free; three would leave under 6 GB). Before each further download, delete the weights of a candidate whose Phase 0–1 results are recorded; a finalist is re-downloaded for Phase 2. Each is under 20 GB, small enough for one GPU, so during Phases 0–1 two can run side by side (one per GPU, ports 8002 and 8003); Phase 2 serves the finalists the way they would be deployed. Gemma 4 and Command R+ each need an operator decision before Phase 0 (§9). Worth adding if Gemma 4 is ported: google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it — Google, Apache 2.0, a mixture-of-experts model with 128 experts, 8 used per token (~4B parameters per token, like Qwen3.6 and the Nemotron models). It shares the 31B's attention layout (head size 512 included), so one port covers most of both; its mixture-of-experts layers are additional work.
docs.title: 3. Candidates and order

docs.text: Factor Value Candidate server GPUs 0–1, which vllm-qwen38.service held until it was stopped and disabled on 2026-10-13 (its weights deleted). Phases 0–1: a candidate under 20 GB runs on one GPU, so two can run side by side (ports 8002 and 8003); Llama 3.3 needs both ( --tensor-parallel-size 2 , port 8002). Phase 2: one finalist at a time, served the way it would be deployed. Production Qwen3.6 stays on GPUs 2–3, port 8001, serving live chat throughout (Command R+ excepted, §9). Launcher Copy config/scripts/vllm_qwen38_volta_serve.sh once per slot. The copy pins GPUs 0,1, --tensor-parallel-size 2 and port 8002, so change all three: GPU 0 slot CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 , --tensor-parallel-size 1 , --port 8002 ; GPU 1 slot CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=1 , --tensor-parallel-size 1 , --port 8003 ; Llama 3.3 CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1 , --tensor-parallel-size 2 , --port 8002 . A candidate on :8003 is reached through its arm config's base_url ; the dev chat dropdown only reaches :8002. In each copy, drop the qwen3_5.py patch bind; set --model , --tool-call-parser (Nemotron: qwen3_coder ; Mistral: mistral plus --tokenizer-mode mistral ; Granite 4.1: hermes or granite4 , chosen in Phase 1.3; Llama: llama3_json plus --chat-template bound from the vLLM repo's examples/ , pinned by commit), --gpu-memory-utilization 0.88 , --max-model-len 32768 . config/ is git-ignored (#286): back the launcher up outside the repo. archi wiring The openai provider slot already points at :8002 ( config/environments/dev.yaml:128 , in the archi-config checkout), so no code change. The benchmark arm config sets services.benchmarking.provider: openai with ollama_url left empty, so the run reads the openai provider block — exactly how the Qwen3.6 and Qwen3.8 arms ran on 2026-10-12 (Qwen3.8's run 1 logged 707 requests to :8002 ). ( provider: local would instead take its endpoint from ollama_url .) Per arm it changes benchmarking.model and that block's base_url ( :8001 , :8002 or :8003 ) and default_model — plus a context_editing.context_windows entry for the candidate's exact model id (as /v1/models reports it). Every arm, Qwen3.6 included, carries the same map — every model id the trial will test, each at 32 768, fixed before the first pilot — because compare_runs.py refuses arms whose context_editing differs (gate G10); the Qwen3.8 arms already carried both ids this way. Without its entry a run has no context limit and long questions come back degraded (6 of 109 the last time). Context window 32 768 for every model, enforced by --max-model-len . Every candidate supports more (128k–256k); holding 32k keeps the comparison fair and the cache budgets in §2–§3 valid. Sampling Pinned identically in every arm, Qwen3.6 included: temperature: 0.3 (the benchmark's value, #701), top_p: 0.95 , top_k: 20 , min_p: 0 , repetition_penalty: 1.0 , thinking off. These are exactly what Qwen3.6 ran with on 2026-10-12 (0.3 from the config, the rest from its generation_config.json ), so the reference stays comparable to those runs. They must be sent explicitly: whatever archi does not send, vLLM fills from each model's own generation_config.json , and the arms would decode differently. temperature and top_p go under the provider's extra_kwargs , the other three under its extra_body . Vendors recommend other settings (Mistral: temperature 0.15); a vendor-settings run is a possible follow-up for the winner, not part of the ranking. Prompt fasrc-docs.md , unchanged. It was written against Qwen models, which may handicap a candidate; a prompt-retune arm is out of scope unless a candidate misses the bar narrowly. Judge Bedrock Claude Sonnet 4.5, 600 s, 6 workers — as in the Qwen3.8 runs.
docs.title: 4. Test bed

docs.text: A candidate moves to the next phase only when every check in the current one passes. Phases 0–1 are hours and about $10–15 of judge spend per candidate; Phase 2 costs ~5–9 h of GPU time and $56–94 of judge spend per candidate (§7), so only the two best candidates out of Phase 1 reach it.
docs.title: 5. Phases

docs.text: # Check Pass 0.1 Weights downloaded to the HF cache provenance chosen per §9 item 6 and recorded; quantization_config.quant_method in config.json read before download and is one the image runs on V100 ( gptq , awq , compressed-tensors ); size recorded; df -h /scratch ≥ 10 GB left 0.2 Server starts at the 0.88 memory cap /v1/models lists the model with max_model_len 32768 0.3 Every checkpoint weight loaded grep -c "not found in params_dict, skip loading" = 0 (the Qwen3.8 silent-garbage tell) 0.4 Memory headroom Record idle and peak nvidia-smi memory per GPU. Pass: idle free memory is no less than production Qwen3.6 shows at the same 0.88 cap (1,624 MiB per GPU on 2026-10-14), and 0.7, the Phase 1.4 pilot and the Phase 2 capacity probe finish with no out-of-memory error — the failure the June margin exists to prevent. A fixed 4 GiB would fail Qwen3.6 itself 0.5 Context-cache pool vLLM 's startup line GPU KV cache size: N tokens ≥ 32 768 (one full-length request; the benchmark asks one question at a time); record N — concurrency is the capacity probe's job (§6) 0.6 fp16 sanity — V100 has no bf16, and these models ship as bf16 five fixed prompts give coherent text: no !!!! , no empty replies, no NaN in logprobs (this also catches a GPTQ act-order checkpoint the fork mis-loads) 0.7 Longest prompt a 30 000-token prompt completes with no out-of-memory error 0.8 Generation speed tokens/s for one stream and for 4 at once, measured the same way on :8001 off-peak for comparison
docs.title: Phase 0 — load and fit (per candidate, pass/fail)

docs.text: Before the first pilot (1.4): copy the Qwen3.8 PREREGISTRATION.md, fill in the whole §6 rule as signed off — the floor, the pilot cut and the ranking — and timestamp it. Nothing in §6 changes once a pilot has run; a change after that point is recorded as a deviation, with the reason. # Check Pass 1.1 chat_template_kwargs: {enable_thinking: false} accepted (no HTTP 400), no thinking text in the reply 1.2 Forced first search: archi pre-fills a search_vectorstore_hybrid call and its result into the history the model's chat template renders the tool-call and tool-result messages; the reply cites the result 1.3 Model-initiated search, streamed the tool parser returns a well-formed call in streaming mode 1.4 30-question pilot (bring up the Phase 2 stack first — the pilot runs in its benchmark container and shares its corpus): a fixed 30-row copy of the bank (set by queries_path in a copy of the arm config) through the benchmark container — the same 30 for every candidate and for Qwen3.6 The harness also appends the anchor questions (on by default, service_benchmark.py:2738 ), so a pilot asks 35 : pick the 30 rows so none duplicates an anchor, which keeps every pilot at exactly 30 + 5. The anchors stay in — they are the §6 anchor floor, judged pass/fail on their own. Give-ups, malformed searches and the cut use the 30 bank rows only ( compare_runs.py leaves anchors out of bank aggregates by default); speed uses every question asked, anchors included, which is what compare_runs.py 's timing block measures. Pass, with some margin: §6's speed floor, ≤ 3 give-ups and ≤ 16 malformed searches of the 30 (§6's limits scaled from 104 rows), every bank question answered ( status: ok ), and every anchor holds. Cut: if more than two candidates pass, only the two with the best answer_correctness on the 30 bank rows go to Phase 2 (~$9–15 and ~1 h per pilot)
docs.title: Phase 1 — through archi (functional)

docs.text: Adapt the Qwen3.8 runner ( /scratch/a2rchi/bench-runs/ragas-qwen38/driver.sh ; its run order, stack path and arm YAML names are hard-coded): one benchmark stack whose data manager never restarts, the benchmark container recreated per run with docker compose … up --no-deps , so every run sees one corpus. Corpus. Either restart the archi-ragas-retrieval-ab stack (containers removed 2026-10-12, volumes kept) with data_manager.reset_collection: false in a copy of its config, or pay one fresh ~83-minute ingest. Record the corpus fingerprint and chunk count before the first run and after the last; a mismatch voids the comparison. Order: Qwen3.6, A, B, B, A, Qwen3.6 (A and B are the two candidates out of Phase 1; with one, Qwen3.6, A, A, Qwen3.6). The finalists are counterbalanced so that drift in the judge, live load or the host over the sequence falls on both equally instead of deciding between them. Each finalist is served the way it would be deployed. If Llama 3.3 (L) is a finalist, its 39.5 GB and the other finalist's (X) checkpoint do not fit together with Phase 0.1's 10 GB margin. The order is then Qwen3.6, X, L, L, X, Qwen3.6: delete X after its first run, download L, delete L after its second run, re-download X. That adds two downloads (time them from Phase 0's and add them to the schedule), unless at least 15 GB is freed elsewhere on /scratch first. Cold start for every candidate run. Restart the candidate's server before each of its runs (a few minutes each), whatever the order. The launchers keep --enable-prefix-caching , so without a restart a second consecutive run could reuse the first run's cached prompts and look faster. Qwen3.6 is production and is not restarted; its two runs are many hours apart, but its cache state cannot be controlled — a known asymmetry that can only flatter Qwen3.6's speed, which is reported, not gated. Fresh Qwen3.6 runs at both ends show net drift as a gap between them instead of letting it hide in the comparison. (The Qwen3.8 runs reused Qwen3.6 runs from earlier that day and had to list that as a weakness.) Load asymmetry. Qwen3.6 on :8001 also serves live chat; the candidates have no other traffic. Run overnight. Any question in a Qwen3.6 run that overlapped a live chat turn (the benchmark container's timestamped log against Postgres turn times) is dropped from the speed figures, on both sides of each Qwen3.6 comparison; the number dropped is reported. Answer-quality scores are kept. The candidates' ranking is unaffected: no finalist shares its server with live traffic. Identifier probe. Replay the 2026-10-13 kempner_rtx prompt ( /scratch/a2rchi/bench-runs/qwen36-name-slip/replay.py , pointed at :8002 ): 200 draws, 8 identical requests at once, temperature 0.3. Qwen3.6 gave 0 / 200 wrong. Capacity probe. 8 bank questions sent at once, 5 rounds, on each server; record p90 time per question. Every one of the 40 requests must return a valid, non-empty answer: an error or timeout fails the floor row instead of counting as a fast response. Production sees several chats at once; a smaller cache pool (§2) shows up here, not in the one-at-a-time benchmark. Pre-registration was frozen before the first pilot (Phase 1); Phase 2 runs under it unchanged.
docs.title: Phase 2 — same-corpus golden-set A/B

docs.text: Commit the launcher and a systemd unit to version control first (#286) — production must be restorable from git. Keep the winner where Phase 2 measured it: a one-GPU finalist on GPU 0 / :8002 ( --tensor-parallel-size 1 ), Llama 3.3 on GPUs 0–1 / :8002 ( --tensor-parallel-size 2 ), under its own enabled systemd unit. Production latency and capacity are then what the trial measured. Moving it later (for example to GPUs 2–3 / :8001 ) is a separate change that repeats the capacity probe and one full run on the new layout. Cut over with no gap. Qwen3.6 keeps serving :8001 while dev.yaml is pointed at the winner: services.chat_app.default_model (which builds the default pipeline, app.py:506 ) and the local provider's default_model and models: → the winner's id, the local provider's base_url → :8002 , its context_windows entry, and the same pinned sampling the benchmark used (§4, #701); remove the Qwen3.8 entry from the openai slot. Redeploy the dev deployment with deploy/scripts/redeploy.sh , which reads deploy/scripts/host.env ( DEPLOYMENT=dev , CONFIG=config/environments/dev.yaml ); confirm the deploy log's config: deploying config/environments/dev.yaml line and that chatbot-dev , postgres-dev and slack-dev were recreated. (Editing dev.yaml and restarting is a no-op — config is re-seeded into Postgres at deploy.) At no point does the running config name a model that no server is serving. Verify end to end on the running deployment before calling adoption done: a live, streamed chat turn that triggers the search tool, and one Slack bot turn. For each, confirm in the Phoenix trace that the request reached the new model id and carries the tool call and its retrieval results, and in Postgres that the turn's persisted trace ( agent_traces.events ) holds the same tool call and result. An HTTP 200 alone is not evidence: a malformed streamed tool call can still return 200. Only after step 4 passes, retire Qwen3.6 with sudo systemctl disable --now vllm-qwen36 — disable, not just stop, so a reboot cannot bring it back. Keep its unit file and weights for one clean week. Rollback: point dev.yaml back at :8001 , sudo systemctl enable --now vllm-qwen36 , redeploy. Update docs/docs/fasrc_archi.md 's host inventory: the winner's model, port, GPUs, launcher and systemd unit, and Qwen3.6 as disabled. Open a new golden-set era in bench_out/banks/golden/report/goldenset_timeline.yaml : numbers before and after a model change are not comparable history.
docs.title: Phase 3 — adoption (only after a pass and a recorded decision)

docs.text: Scored on the 104 bank questions (anchors excluded, as in the Qwen3.8 comparison). Each question's score is the mean of that model's two runs; differences are paired by question over questions scored in every run being compared. 1. Usability floor — every candidate run must clear every row. Absolute numbers, because the move is mandatory: the question is "what is the slowest, least reliable chat we would ship?", not "how close to Qwen3.6". The proposals below are about the worst Qwen3.6 has done plus a margin; Qwen3.8's numbers are shown for scale. The speed rows count every question asked, anchors included (what compare_runs.py 's timing block measures); the other rows count the 104 bank rows. The harness records a question that raises an error as a failed row and carries on ( service_benchmark.py:2507 ), and the paired analysis drops unscored questions, so the "answered" row is what stops a failing candidate from looking faster and cleaner. Measure Qwen3.6 (2026-10-12) Qwen3.8 (2026-10-12) Proposed floor Mean seconds per question 29.9 / 34.6 71.8 / 63.4 ≤ 60 p90 seconds per question 48.2 / 70.8 253.4 / 188.4 ≤ 150 Give-up answers (counted as in model_subsets.py ) 4 / 5 16 / 12 ≤ 8 Malformed search calls ( No query found. ) 43 / 42 93 / 108 ≤ 55 Degraded answers (context overflow) 0 / 0 0 / 0 0 Bank questions answered ( status: ok ) 104 / 104 104 / 104 all; a run with failed rows is rerun once, and a question that fails again fails the floor Identifier probe ( kempner_rtx ), wrong spellings 0 / 200 — ≤ 2 / 200 Capacity probe (8 questions at once × 5 rounds) measured in Phase 2 — 40 of 40 answered, non-empty; p90 ≤ 180 s Anchors: the should_refuse anchor refused, every easy_retrieve anchor cites its expected source checked on the bracketing runs — all hold, in every run 2. Ranking — among candidates that clear the floor. Primary: answer_correctness , candidate against candidate, computed as follows. compare_runs.py compares one run file against one baseline file and cannot average two runs per model, so the primary statistic comes from a small analysis script adapted from the Qwen3.8 comparison's model_subsets.py , frozen with the pre-registration (its file hash recorded there): per question, each finalist's score is the mean of its two runs; d = A − B per question, over the bank questions scored in all four finalist runs; SE = standard deviation of d / √n; σ = the larger of the two finalists' run-to-run spread (the absolute difference between a model's two run means), as in the Qwen3.8 comparison; a difference counts only if |mean d| exceeds both 2·SE and 2·σ, and the per-run pairs (A run 1 vs B run 1, A run 2 vs B run 2, from compare_runs.py ) agree in sign. compare_runs.py still runs on every per-run pair, for its validity gates (G3–G10) and the G8 report below. Inside that noise, the tie is broken in order by faithfulness , mean seconds per question, give-up answers, then the simpler operation (fewer GPUs, no image patches). With a single candidate in Phase 2, there is nothing to rank: it is adopted if it clears the floor. compare_runs.py 's G8 row (anchors, plus "no other metric regressed past one noise unit") is reported for the finalist pair, with the runner-up as baseline and --noise-runs set to the runner-up's two runs, so every metric has a noise floor; where a metric's two-run σ is 0, --noise-floor takes the larger of the two finalists' two-run spreads for it, recorded as a deviation (the Qwen3.8 comparison's procedure). Without a floor, G8 skips that metric and can read clean when it was never tested. If the correctness winner shows a G8 regression on another metric, the choice goes to the operator with both rows in front of them, recorded in the ledger — it is not automatic either way. G8 is not a hard gate here because on 2026-10-12 it raised an alarm on Qwen3.6 against its own second run (easy-anchor scores, and answer_correctness against a two-run noise estimate of 0.0025). Against Qwen3.6, G8 is reported as part of the cost of the policy. 3. Cost of the policy — reported, not gated. Each candidate minus Qwen3.6 on every RAGAS metric, source accuracy, speed and judge cost per run, so the operator can say what the move cost. context_precision and context_recall can move too: the model writes the search queries. If no candidate clears the floor: the operator chooses between relaxing the floor; the Gemma 4 port (§9); and the Anthropic standby already configured in dev.yaml ( default_provider: anthropic , US-developed) — which sends every question off the host and is billed per token, so it is a decision, not a default.
docs.title: 6. Decision rule (frozen before the first pilot)

docs.text: What costs money. Only the judge — the Bedrock Claude Sonnet 4.5 model that grades each answer. GPU time is on-prem and carries no per-run charge; downloads are free. Judge prices are Bedrock list ($3.30 / $16.50 per million input / output tokens); HUIT billing may differ. Wall time is the model's answering time (109 × seconds per question) plus judging and start-up, which took 55–131 min in the four measured runs. A finalist that meets the §6 speed floor (mean ≤ 60 s) answers in under 1 h 50 min, so no Phase 2 candidate run should exceed ~4 h. Run Questions Wall time (est.) Judge cost (est.) docs.title: 8. Ledger

docs.text: Made (operator, 2026-10-13): - The move off Qwen is policy; candidates cannot be Chinese-developed. The winner is the best allowed model that clears the usability floor (§1, §6). - Qwen3.8 stopped and disabled; its weights deleted. Open: 1. The usability floor in §6 — confirm or change the numbers before the first pilot, when the rule is frozen: what is the slowest, least reliable chat you would ship? 2. Gemma 4: fund a separate spike — port the Gemma 4 architecture into the Volta fork and (most likely) extend its attention kernel to head size 512, with its own estimate and the rebuild risk of #286 (the image has no build recipe) — covering both 31B and 26B-A4B; or drop Gemma 4. 3. Command R+: recommend dropping. Trialling it needs all of: a tool parser written for its output format, a trial window with production failed over to the Anthropic standby (it needs all four GPUs), deleting more of the model cache, and a legal reading of CC-BY-NC for institutional use — for a model two generations old. 4. Fallback if nothing clears the floor (§6): relax the floor, fund the Gemma 4 port, or accept the off-host Anthropic standby. 5. License sign-off for the winner. Apache 2.0, OpenMDW-1.1 and the Llama 3.3 Community License are routine; the NVIDIA Nemotron Open Model License (Nemotron 3 Nano) adds an attribution notice and terminates if the user brings an IP suit against NVIDIA. 6. Who made the 4-bit weights. The policy is about who made the model, and a 4-bit checkpoint is the developer's weights re-packaged by whoever quantized them. Every checkpoint in §3 except Google's and Red Hat's comes from an individual Hugging Face account. Production's Qwen3.6 file ( palmfuture/… ) is one too, so this is not a new exposure, but it should be a decision. Options per candidate: a vendor-published 4-bit where one exists (Red Hat's Llama 3.3); otherwise quantize in-house from the developer's official repo with llm-compressor or GPTQModel on GPUs 0–1 (estimate: hours for a 24–32B model, longer for 70B); or accept the community checkpoint. Record the choice in the ledger.
docs.title: 9. Decisions

docs.text: HarvardKey + Archi RBAC — decisions, and the open question that blocks them Status: ON HOLD as of 2026-09-01. No spec written. No code written. The hold exists because question 1 in Questions for Harvard IAM can invalidate the protocol choice. What this document asks of you: confirm question 1 with Harvard IAM, or tell us if a decision below is wrong. Everything else is ready to turn into a spec. Decisions taken (2026-09-01) Scope of protection: every user signs in with a HarvardKey to use chat. Named roles gate the privileged surface — upload, config, evaluations, alerts, and admin. Role source: Harvard central groups (Grouper), not a list that Archi keeps. That retires the two lists Archi keeps today: services.chat_app.alerts.managers (defect 7) and users.is_admin as a role source (defect 3). Protocol: OpenID Connect, and Archi reads the memberOf claim. Group-to-role map: an explicit map in config.yaml , read by a new src/utils/rbac/group_mapper.py . No naming convention. No second role store in Postgres, so an API bearer token carries the default role only (defect 3). Archi already owns the whole permission layer, so none of this builds one. src/utils/rbac/ holds a role registry with inheritance, 26 permissions in a Permission enum, route decorators, and audit logs. src/interfaces/chat_app/app.py:3353 already registers a generic OpenID Connect client through authlib. The layer is dormant: the FASRC dev deployment sets auth.enabled: false . The one thing that does not fit is the role source. src/utils/rbac/jwt_parser.py reads resource_access.<app>.roles , a Keycloak claim shape inherited from CERN SSO upstream. HarvardKey sends no such claim under either protocol. So this work replaces the role-extraction function, plus one small change in sso_callback . Today the callback fetches UserInfo into a local variable only when the ID token carries no claims ( app.py:3467-3470 ), then calls get_user_roles(token, …) with the token alone ( :3478 ). If IAM answers question 2 with "UserInfo only", the mapper never sees memberOf unless the callback fetches UserInfo whenever the ID token lacks the claim and hands the result to the mapper explicitly. Why the protocol choice needs confirmation Two Harvard pages disagree. The HarvardKey Attributes Available Table (sheet id 1Fbv8HldQ0a9VGwEyMZevyAuqNtpv0qCJ0-iwzCOXC0c , gid 848693615 ) lists memberOf ( urn:oid:1.3.6.1.4.1.19376.1.2.4.1.6 ) as available in SAML and in OIDC , at all risk levels, with no riders required. Selecting a HarvardKey Authentication Protocol says OIDC supports only first name, last name, display name, nickname, email, profile URL, and preferred username, and it directs applications that need group membership to SAML. If the table is right, Archi reuses the OIDC client it already has. If the article is right, the work grows by a Shibboleth service provider: a new container, an SP keypair with rotation, xmlsec1 in the image, and metadata exchange with IAM. Questions for Harvard IAM Send to iam_help@harvard.edu . Can a HarvardKey OIDC application receive the memberOf attribute? The Attributes Available Table says yes. The protocol-selection article implies no. Which applies to a new integration? If OIDC can receive it: which scope must the client request, and does the claim arrive in the ID token, from the UserInfo endpoint, or both? What is the value format? The table says "Grouper filter string". Is that a full path such as harvard:org:fasrc:archi-admins , or a flat name? Does it arrive as a JSON array? The table populates memberOf only "for groups provisioned to HLDAP or UNIVAD". What is the process to provision a new custom Grouper group to one of those, and how long does it take? Can one application use several custom groups — one for each privilege tier, for example archi-admins and archi-operators — while the application's own authorization group stays broad enough that a non-privileged person still signs in? Over OIDC, which claim is the recommended stable unique identifier? The table marks harvardEduNetId unavailable in OIDC. Archi keys users.id on the OIDC sub claim today ( src/interfaces/chat_app/app.py:3482 ). Is sub stable and unique for one person across sessions and a name change? If not, is eduPersonPrincipalName the right key, and does it stay constant across a name change? Is a *.rc.fas.harvard.edu host acceptable for the redirect URI? Can one registration carry separate development and production redirect URIs, or do we register two applications? Existing defects this work must fix Items 1 to 3 were found 2026-09-01 against origin/dev . Items 4 to 7 came out of the review of PR #398 the same day, verified against the same tree. All seven are latent today, because auth.enabled: false on the dev deployment. No HTTPS, no proxy trust, and an insecure session cookie. The chat app runs the bare Flask server ( src/interfaces/chat_app/app.py:3838 ). Harvard registers one exact HTTPS redirect URI. Behind a TLS proxy, url_for("sso_callback", _external=True) emits http:// unless the app trusts X-Forwarded-Proto . Nothing in the repository does. docs/docs/advanced_setup_deploy.md:151 documents an nginx example that nothing deploys. The same setup leaves SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE unset ( app.py:2797-2801 ), so once TLS terminates upstream, the HarvardKey-backed session cookie still travels in plaintext to the published port. The code half of the fix is proxy trust plus that flag; the infrastructure half is prerequisite 4. No explanation for a refused user. sso_callback catches the provider error, calls flash("Authentication failed: …") , and redirects to /login ( app.py:3536-3537 ). login starts SSO only when the request carries ?method=sso ( :3398 ), so there is no redirect loop. But it renders landing.html ( :3426 ), and that template has no flashed-messages block — only login.html has one, and the chat app never renders it. The user lands on the plain login page with no reason. Harvard's own page warns that OIDC returns unauthorized users to the application, which must handle the error itself. Two role sources disagree. The browser path reads roles from the token. The API path derives them from one boolean — ["admin"] if user.is_admin else [default_role] at src/interfaces/chat_app/openai_compat.py:159-161 . The same person gets admin in a browser and base-user through an API token. A bearer request carries no OIDC token, no UserInfo response, and no memberOf ( openai_compat.py:142-161 ), so the group mapper cannot serve it, and decision 4 rules out a role store in Postgres. Resolution: bearer requests take the default role only, and the is_admin shortcut goes. /v1 checks only chat:query ( openai_compat.py:106 , :166 ), so no API caller loses a permission it uses today. The alternative — caching the last resolved roles on the users row at each browser login — is a second role store with a revocation lag, and decision 4 rejects it. The role registry fails open. With no auth_roles block, load_rbac_config() returns a base-user role with permissions: ["*"] ( src/utils/rbac/registry.py:465-479 ), and the rendered config carries no auth_roles unless the deployment supplies one ( src/cli/templates/base-config.yaml:148-150 ). Turn HarvardKey on in that state and every signed-in user holds every permission. With auth.enabled: true , a missing or empty registry must refuse to start, and the deployment must ship a complete auth_roles block that names every role in the group-to-role map. Agent-spec writes are gated by login alone. /api/agents POST and DELETE and /api/agents/active POST are registered with require_auth only ( app.py:3088-3104 ), while every other privileged write goes through require_perm : update_config takes config:modify ( :2935 ), uploads take upload:* , the database viewer takes database:admin . The three agent handlers ( :4181 , :4221 , :4340 ) write shared agent specs to disk and set the active agent in Postgres. Once every HarvardKey holder can sign in, any of them can change the system prompt and tool set for everyone. These routes must take config:modify . The data-manager service sits outside the chat app's auth and fails open. It is a separate Flask app with its own basic auth. services.data_manager.auth.enabled defaults to false ( src/cli/templates/base-config.yaml:161-163 ), require_admin passes every request through in that state ( src/interfaces/uploader_app/app.py:191-203 ), and the compose template publishes its port on the host ( src/cli/templates/base-compose.yaml:81-82 ). HarvardKey on the chat app changes none of that: a caller who can reach the port can upload and ingest with no role at all. This document keeps the data-manager outside HarvardKey; production turns its own auth on and keeps the port off any reachable interface (prerequisite 6). A username allowlist bypasses alerts:manage . is_alert_manager() grants alert management when the session username appears in services.chat_app.alerts.managers ( src/interfaces/chat_app/service_alerts.py:44-61 ), whatever the roles say. Removing a person from the Grouper group would not revoke it while the name stays in the config. Decision 2 retires the list: alert management flows from alerts:manage alone, and the config key goes. Harvard mechanics worth keeping Harvard splits access control in two, and only one half depends on the protocol. Authorization groups sit on the identity-provider side. They are mandatory: every HarvardKey application names at least one, and Harvard tests membership before it returns the user. The stated reason is that a HarvardKey keeps working after a person leaves Harvard. This half needs no Archi code. Attribute release is optional and privacy-reviewed. It supplies the data that drives Archi roles. Affiliation attributes ( eduPersonAffiliation , harvardEduPersonAffiliation , eduPersonScopedAffiliation ) are SAML-only, and most need GDPR and personal-data riders at risk level 3 to 4. Group membership is not in that category. That distinction is what makes OIDC viable here: Archi's permissions are group-shaped, not affiliation-shaped. config:modify does not follow from "staff" or "FAS". It follows from "this named person operates Archi", which is a Grouper group. harvardEduNetId and displayName also do not cross OIDC. Archi keys users on the OIDC sub claim today and keeps doing so until IAM answers question 6; whether sub or eduPersonPrincipalName is the stable key is that question, not a decision here. The display name falls back to mail . Prerequisites that no code change removes HKAR registration. Submit the Application Integration Form with a benefits-eligible Harvard sponsor, the OIDC redirect URI, and an attribute request for the memberOf release bundle. Annual attestation follows. At least one authorization group. Mandatory. Pick IAM reference groups, or ask IAM to build a custom group. One Grouper group for each privileged Archi role, provisioned to HLDAP or UNIVAD. A group that exists in Grouper but is not provisioned there releases nothing. TLS on a registered hostname in front of the deployment. This is the infrastructure half of defect 1; the code half (proxy trust and SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE ) stays in the defect list. The answer to question 1. This one can invalidate the protocol choice, so it comes before implementation, not during. Data-manager auth on, and its port off the public interface. Set services.data_manager.auth.enabled: true , and keep data_manager_port_host off any interface a browser can reach (defect 6). Next step Send the seven questions. Then write the spec against the confirmed protocol. Milestone note: issue #81 (production readiness) sits in v2026.11.0 , and this work reads as a gate for that release.

If IAM answers question 2 with "UserInfo only", the mapper never sees memberOf unless the callback fetches UserInfo whenever the ID token lacks the claim and hands the result to the mapper explicitly.
docs.title: Decisions taken (2026-09-01)

docs.text: Two Harvard pages disagree. The HarvardKey Attributes Available Table (sheet id 1Fbv8HldQ0a9VGwEyMZevyAuqNtpv0qCJ0-iwzCOXC0c , gid 848693615 ) lists memberOf ( urn:oid:1.3.6.1.4.1.19376.1.2.4.1.6 ) as available in SAML and in OIDC , at all risk levels, with no riders required. Selecting a HarvardKey Authentication Protocol says OIDC supports only first name, last name, display name, nickname, email, profile URL, and preferred username, and it directs applications that need group membership to SAML. If the table is right, Archi reuses the OIDC client it already has. If the article is right, the work grows by a Shibboleth service provider: a new container, an SP keypair with rotation, xmlsec1 in the image, and metadata exchange with IAM.
docs.title: Why the protocol choice needs confirmation

docs.text: Send to iam_help@harvard.edu . Can a HarvardKey OIDC application receive the memberOf attribute? The Attributes Available Table says yes. The protocol-selection article implies no. Which applies to a new integration? If OIDC can receive it: which scope must the client request, and does the claim arrive in the ID token, from the UserInfo endpoint, or both? What is the value format? The table says "Grouper filter string". Is that a full path such as harvard:org:fasrc:archi-admins , or a flat name? Does it arrive as a JSON array? The table populates memberOf only "for groups provisioned to HLDAP or UNIVAD". What is the process to provision a new custom Grouper group to one of those, and how long does it take? Can one application use several custom groups — one for each privilege tier, for example archi-admins and archi-operators — while the application's own authorization group stays broad enough that a non-privileged person still signs in? Over OIDC, which claim is the recommended stable unique identifier? The table marks harvardEduNetId unavailable in OIDC. Archi keys users.id on the OIDC sub claim today ( src/interfaces/chat_app/app.py:3482 ). Is sub stable and unique for one person across sessions and a name change? If not, is eduPersonPrincipalName the right key, and does it stay constant across a name change? Is a *.rc.fas.harvard.edu host acceptable for the redirect URI? Can one registration carry separate development and production redirect URIs, or do we register two applications?
docs.title: Questions for Harvard IAM

docs.text: Items 1 to 3 were found 2026-09-01 against origin/dev . Items 4 to 7 came out of the review of PR #398 the same day, verified against the same tree. All seven are latent today, because auth.enabled: false on the dev deployment. No HTTPS, no proxy trust, and an insecure session cookie. The chat app runs the bare Flask server ( src/interfaces/chat_app/app.py:3838 ). Harvard registers one exact HTTPS redirect URI. Behind a TLS proxy, url_for("sso_callback", _external=True) emits http:// unless the app trusts X-Forwarded-Proto . Nothing in the repository does. docs/docs/advanced_setup_deploy.md:151 documents an nginx example that nothing deploys. The same setup leaves SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE unset ( app.py:2797-2801 ), so once TLS terminates upstream, the HarvardKey-backed session cookie still travels in plaintext to the published port. The code half of the fix is proxy trust plus that flag; the infrastructure half is prerequisite 4. No explanation for a refused user. sso_callback catches the provider error, calls flash("Authentication failed: …") , and redirects to /login ( app.py:3536-3537 ). login starts SSO only when the request carries ?method=sso ( :3398 ), so there is no redirect loop. But it renders landing.html ( :3426 ), and that template has no flashed-messages block — only login.html has one, and the chat app never renders it. The user lands on the plain login page with no reason. Harvard's own page warns that OIDC returns unauthorized users to the application, which must handle the error itself. Two role sources disagree. The browser path reads roles from the token. The API path derives them from one boolean — ["admin"] if user.is_admin else [default_role] at src/interfaces/chat_app/openai_compat.py:159-161 . The same person gets admin in a browser and base-user through an API token. A bearer request carries no OIDC token, no UserInfo response, and no memberOf ( openai_compat.py:142-161 ), so the group mapper cannot serve it, and decision 4 rules out a role store in Postgres. Resolution: bearer requests take the default role only, and the is_admin shortcut goes. /v1 checks only chat:query ( openai_compat.py:106 , :166 ), so no API caller loses a permission it uses today. The alternative — caching the last resolved roles on the users row at each browser login — is a second role store with a revocation lag, and decision 4 rejects it. The role registry fails open. With no auth_roles block, load_rbac_config() returns a base-user role with permissions: ["*"] ( src/utils/rbac/registry.py:465-479 ), and the rendered config carries no auth_roles unless the deployment supplies one ( src/cli/templates/base-config.yaml:148-150 ). Turn HarvardKey on in that state and every signed-in user holds every permission. With auth.enabled: true , a missing or empty registry must refuse to start, and the deployment must ship a complete auth_roles block that names every role in the group-to-role map. Agent-spec writes are gated by login alone. /api/agents POST and DELETE and /api/agents/active POST are registered with require_auth only ( app.py:3088-3104 ), while every other privileged write goes through require_perm : update_config takes config:modify ( :2935 ), uploads take upload:* , the database viewer takes database:admin . The three agent handlers ( :4181 , :4221 , :4340 ) write shared agent specs to disk and set the active agent in Postgres. Once every HarvardKey holder can sign in, any of them can change the system prompt and tool set for everyone. These routes must take config:modify . The data-manager service sits outside the chat app's auth and fails open. It is a separate Flask app with its own basic auth. services.data_manager.auth.enabled defaults to false ( src/cli/templates/base-config.yaml:161-163 ), require_admin passes every request through in that state ( src/interfaces/uploader_app/app.py:191-203 ), and the compose template publishes its port on the host ( src/cli/templates/base-compose.yaml:81-82 ). HarvardKey on the chat app changes none of that: a caller who can reach the port can upload and ingest with no role at all. This document keeps the data-manager outside HarvardKey; production turns its own auth on and keeps the port off any reachable interface (prerequisite 6). A username allowlist bypasses alerts:manage . is_alert_manager() grants alert management when the session username appears in services.chat_app.alerts.managers ( src/interfaces/chat_app/service_alerts.py:44-61 ), whatever the roles say. Removing a person from the Grouper group would not revoke it while the name stays in the config. Decision 2 retires the list: alert management flows from alerts:manage alone, and the config key goes.
docs.title: Existing defects this work must fix

docs.text: Harvard splits access control in two, and only one half depends on the protocol. Authorization groups sit on the identity-provider side. They are mandatory: every HarvardKey application names at least one, and Harvard tests membership before it returns the user. The stated reason is that a HarvardKey keeps working after a person leaves Harvard. This half needs no Archi code. Attribute release is optional and privacy-reviewed. It supplies the data that drives Archi roles. Affiliation attributes ( eduPersonAffiliation , harvardEduPersonAffiliation , eduPersonScopedAffiliation ) are SAML-only, and most need GDPR and personal-data riders at risk level 3 to 4. Group membership is not in that category. That distinction is what makes OIDC viable here: Archi's permissions are group-shaped, not affiliation-shaped. config:modify does not follow from "staff" or "FAS". It follows from "this named person operates Archi", which is a Grouper group. harvardEduNetId and displayName also do not cross OIDC. Archi keys users on the OIDC sub claim today and keeps doing so until IAM answers question 6; whether sub or eduPersonPrincipalName is the stable key is that question, not a decision here. The display name falls back to mail .
docs.title: Harvard mechanics worth keeping

docs.text: HKAR registration. Submit the Application Integration Form with a benefits-eligible Harvard sponsor, the OIDC redirect URI, and an attribute request for the memberOf release bundle. Annual attestation follows. At least one authorization group. Mandatory. Pick IAM reference groups, or ask IAM to build a custom group. One Grouper group for each privileged Archi role, provisioned to HLDAP or UNIVAD. A group that exists in Grouper but is not provisioned there releases nothing. TLS on a registered hostname in front of the deployment. This is the infrastructure half of defect 1; the code half (proxy trust and SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE ) stays in the defect list. The answer to question 1. This one can invalidate the protocol choice, so it comes before implementation, not during. Data-manager auth on, and its port off the public interface. Set services.data_manager.auth.enabled: true , and keep data_manager_port_host off any interface a browser can reach (defect 6).
